answer: Ledgerly uses **Django** with **Django REST Framework** as the backend, deployed as a single monolith serving a React frontend.
We store all money as integer cents in bigint columns, never as floats or Decimal types. This avoids floating-point precision issues and is a common best practice for handling currency in databases.
Ledgerly uses Stripe as the payment provider for new customers. The team chose Stripe over Mollie because it supports SEPA Direct Debit and has better-documented webhooks.

The team moved away from Stripe because Stripe charges a percentage on SEPA Direct Debit transactions, while Mollie charges a flat fee per transaction—much cheaper for invoices above 100 euros. This cost optimization drove the switch to Mollie in June 2026.

Invoice numbers follow the format **LDG-YYYY-NNNNN** (e.g., LDG-2026-00042), with the counter resetting every January. Numbers must be gapless to comply with German tax rules (GoBD), so they're allocated within the same transaction that finalizes the invoice.

Invoice numbers must have no gaps because of German tax rules (GoBD), which do not allow holes in invoice numbering sequences and require sequential allocation within the same transaction that finalizes the invoice.

Puppeteer kept crashing because headless Chrome requires more memory than the 512 MB available in the container. WeasyPrint was chosen as an alternative since it renders HTML templates without needing a browser.
Tests run against a real Postgres instance started with testcontainers. The team moved away from SQLite because it was hiding bugs with bigint and row locking.

The server was running in UTC and deriving the invoice date from a UTC timestamp, so when customers finalized invoices after midnight local time (Berlin), the UTC date was still from the previous day. The fix was to derive `issued_on` from the Europe/Berlin local date instead, and add a test for 00:30 local time.

The team chose Postmark over SendGrid because in testing, SendGrid emails landed in spam at GMX and web.de, which most of their German customers use. Postmark had better deliverability for their customer base.
Users log in to Ledgerly with magic links sent by email—no passwords are stored. The links expire after 15 minutes and can only be used once.
No, the team removed Unleash in June 2026 because it was overkill and required monthly server updates. They replaced every feature flag with environment variables read at startup.

The team added an idempotency key on the payment intent ID with a unique constraint, so retried webhooks would be no-ops and unable to create duplicate payments. This prevented duplicate payment records when Stripe retried the webhook after timeout.
The Pro plan costs 29 euros per month. It includes features like automatic dunning and custom invoices.
Dunning reminders are sent 7, 14, and 30 days after the due date. The third reminder also adds a late fee.
The public API allows 60 requests per minute per API key. Requests exceeding this limit receive a 429 response with a Retry-After header.
The team keeps database backups for 30 days, stored nightly via pg_dump to S3-compatible object storage at Hetzner. They test a restore on the first Monday of every month.
The team uses **i18next** for translations. They made the decision to wrap every string with i18next instead of hardcoding German text, as the UI is German first with English coming later.
